extracted.intended_audience: researchers, grant reviewers, and research-funder staff concerned with bias in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A literature/resource page compiling research on different forms of bias in peer review (disability, language, gender, sexual orientation, race, age/career stage, institutional, etc.) and on strategies to mitigate those biases. Useful for people designing, evaluating, or training for fairer peer-review and grant-review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to explicit and implicit bias against people with disabilities in peer review, participation, funding, and academic careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists numerous sources on disability and ableism in academia and peer review (e.g., Iezzoni 2018 'Explicit disability bias in peer review'; Inkle 2018 'Unreasonable Adjustments'; Swenor et al. 2019 'A decade of decline: Grant funding for researchers with disabilities'). Use these works to identify ways disability manifests as disadvantage in review, disclosure and accommodation issues, and structural barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, institutional, age and career-stage bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases arising from language of publication, institutional affiliation/prestige, researcher age, and career stage that affect review and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References documenting linguistic and institutional biases (e.g., studies on francophone research dissemination, linguistic bias in reviewing — Politzer-Ahles et al. 2020; Office of the Commissioner on promotion of official languages). Use these to assess whether review criteria or processes disadvantage non-dominant languages, less-prestigious institutions, or early/late career researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic biases affecting people of different genders in peer review, hiring, grants, citations, invitations to referee, recommendation letters, and career outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites empirical and review literature on gender bias and interventions (e.g., Helmer et al. 2017; Carnes et al. 2015; Lerback & Hanson 2017; Kaatz et al. 2014; Tricco et al. 2017). Includes work on gendered wording, citation disparities, and gender-neutral policies' unintended effects. Use findings to evaluate gendered effects and candidate- vs.-science-driven sources of disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias based on sexual orientation and gender identity (LGBTQ/2SLGBTQIA+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases that disadvantage sexual and gender minority scholars in workplace climate, peer review, funding processes, and scholarly visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes systematic reviews and empirical studies documenting discrimination and microaggressions (e.g., Badgett et al.; Beagan et al. 2021; Freeman 2019; Nelson et al. 2022; The Inclusion Group for Equity in Research in STEMM 2019). Use these to identify climate- and process-level barriers and to justify inclusion-focused interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias in the peer review process (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various forms of bias that can affect peer review reliability, fairness, validity and generalizability (race, gender, nepotism, positive-outcome bias, commensuration bias, conservatism, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References broad treatments of peer-review bias and its effects (e.g., Lee et al. 2013 'Bias in peer review'; Smith 2006 'Peer review: a flawed process'; Marsh et al. 2008 on improving reliability, validity, bias). Also cites studies on nepotism and sexism (Wennerås & Wold 1997), commensuration bias (Lee 2015), and structural racism in journals (Merchant et al. 2021). Use these to evaluate how process design contributes to systemic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit bias and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that unconscious/implicit associations influence evaluative decisions and that these can be measured and targeted (e.g., using the Implicit Association Test) and are relevant to reviewer judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites foundational IAT literature and meta-analyses (Greenwald et al. 1998; Greenwald et al. 2009) and intervention studies (Lai et al. 2014). Use these sources to justify implicit-bias training, IAT-informed diagnostics, and evidence-based interventions while noting limitations of predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive-outcome and publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency for peer review and editorial decisions to favor positive or novel results, which can distort evaluation of research quality and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions randomized trials testing for positive-outcome bias (Emerson et al. 2010). Use such work to assess whether evaluation criteria inadvertently privilege 'positive' outcomes and to design blind or structured review mechanisms to counteract this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism, risk-aversion, and topic-choice bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias toward conservative, low-risk topics or approaches and bias against research topics associated with particular groups, which can reduce funding/citation rates for certain researchers or topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites work on conservatism and risk-taking in review (Luukkonen 2012) and on topic choice contributing to award disparities (Hoppe et al. 2019). Use to evaluate whether review criteria reward safe projects and disadvantage novel or population-specific topic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation strategies for bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence-based strategies and interventions to prevent or reduce bias in peer review and related evaluation processes (training, anonymization, reviewer diversity, inclusive metrics, policy changes, structured criteria, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes systematic reviews and intervention studies (Tricco et al. 2017; Carnes et al. 2015; Anderson et al. 2015; Lai et al. 2014), and proposals for inclusive metrics and structural change (Davies et al. 2021 'Promoting inclusive metrics', Marsh et al. 2008). Use these sources to design concrete interventions: bias training, structured scoring rubrics, anonymized review where feasible, diversify reviewer pools, and adapt metrics of success to be more inclusive.
